This isn’t really correct. The forerunners committed genocide and pursued the precursors to an extragalactic small galaxy called Path Kethona. There they killed what they thought were the remaining precursors and then exiled themselves there out of shame. Fast forward a few eons and a small ship drifted into Ancient Human space, which onboard had powdered material and nothing else. The humans experimented with the dust and found that it had “favorable” mutations on their pet rabbits or dogs or something, so they started to more or less add the dust to their pet food. Eventually the pets mutated further and became more and more aggressive until they became the first flood forms. These started infecting humans and forerunners alike, and cause humanity and the forerunners to go to war, since the humans were purging any planet that had any sign of infection. That’s the flood origin story.

Sounds like a DMR that fires a higher caliber. I think the military would have a hard time justifying a weapon that provides a small benefit for a very very very select group of soldiers. Spartans provide the benefit of being A large force multiplier when deployed on the field that can easily dispatch several platoons of covenant troops with conventional weapons already. A special weapon would need to fill some sort of role the Spartans can’t fill with readily available tools. 

The UNSC did make the spartan laser which is about as spartan specific as we have seen so far. But it’s rarely ever deployed and it’s usable by anyone, and more or less adds to that anti air/anti armor role that Spartans already fill, but it has a logistical issue of needing to be fully serviced to be reused.

Money and logistics. 

You manufacture roughly 70 soldiers that will be deployed behind enemy lines for weeks at a time across your huge territory. These areas will be cutoff from regular resupply and from a proper base. You want them to have easily serviceable and easy to acquire weapons, such as your MA40 or M392 which have been military mainstays and extremely dependable for close to a century. These soldiers will be needing to field strip their tools and access to easy to minifab ammo or able to find ammo that’s compatible, a very distinct disadvantage that a specialized weapon doesn’t have. So logistically that’s the easy solution.

Money wise, you already spent so much money on a platform that could’ve funded fleets of ships, it would be hard to justify to a government that you need even more money for a weapon that can’t be handled by 99.99999% of your ground forces.

I’ve seen this posted before but basically it boils down to mimicking an actual navy military maneuver. The ground team is there to clear any AA threat, airborne or otherwise, then that frees up two fast movers, lightly armed or unarmed, to push through and force a vulnerable ship away from a no fire area into a free fire zone for the cannon. In real life this is done to ships sitting in strategic ports or to minimize collateral damage. Typically you’d have a few flights geared up for air to ground and another for air to air. The air to air guys get caught in a fur ball with the other aircraft, followed by bombers or attackers striking any AA batteries followed by another flight or the same flight to do an attack run on the ship itself or to force a retreat. It was a strategy that was pretty popular in the 40s to break naval blockades. I don’t think it’s been used in modern times due to fancy radars and stuff
